newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran, Pakistan say force will not end Afghan crisis.
newsitem.headline: Iran, Pakistan say force will not end Afghan crisis.

text.p: Iran and Pakistan, at odds over the war in Afghanistan, said that the use of force would not settle the crisis in the war-torn country, the official Iranian news agency IRNA reported.
IRNA said late on Monday that Iran's President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and visiting Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif discussed the Afghan crisis during talks in Tehran.
"We believe that the differences, war and bloodshed will yield no results for any of the factions engaged in the conflict (in Afghanistan)," IRNA quoted Rafsanjani as telling Sharif.

"The president added that the only basic way and a permanent solution to the ongoing crisis is the participation of all factions based on the the interests of the Afghan people who have suffered through the crisis," IRNA added.
It quoted Sharif as saying at the talks that "Pakistan is of the opinion that military solutions cannot be successful in any one of the regional crises."
"According to him (Sharif) the government of Pakistan has decided to open a new phase in promotion of relations with Islamic Iran," IRNA added.
Relations between Iran and Pakistan, longstanding partners in the regional Economic Cooperation Organisation, have been strained by policy differences over Afghanistan.
Tehran and Islamabad both say they favour U.N. peace efforts aimed at formation of a broad-based Afghan government including all the ethnic, political and religious groups.
But Iran, deeply suspicious of the purist Islamic Taleban militia that has ruled Kabul since September, still recognises the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani.
Pakistan, which denies Afghan opposition charges that it supports the Taleban, became the first country formally to recognise the movement's government on May 25.
Iran has expressed concern about the Taleban's religious militancy which it says has given Islam a bad name.
